newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE - Housing promise could fail Singapore party.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Housing promise could fail Singapore party.

text.p: Singapore's rulers may find use of a key incentive to vote -- renovation of public housing estates -- wins only selective and short-term support in impending elections, analysts and opposition politicians say.

More than 80 percent of the population live in state-subsidised flats and ministers of the People's Action Party (PAP) government have been touring constituencies telling voters they cannot expect lavish renovation and development projects if they send an opposition politician to parliament.

Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong told voters he would respect the voters' choice if they elected an opposition candidate, but added: "Then you'll be left behind, then in 20, 30 years' time, the whole of Singapore will be bustling away and your estate, through your own choice, will be left behind.
"They become slums. That's my message," Goh said.
That comment sparked a sharp exchange of words -- not with Singapore voters, but with the U.S. State Department.

"We understand that ruling party candidates, including the prime minister, have warned that constituencies that elect opposition candidates will receive low priority in extensive government plans to upgrade housing facilities," the State Department said.
"We believe that voters everywhere should be able to vote without fear of repercussions from government as a result of their responsibilities as citizens."
Goh told reporters in reponse: "I can tell you I was furious, I was flabbergasted, floored...
"This is a local election and what we offer the people as a programme is no more different from what any candidate anywhere else will offer their electorate," Goh said.
Information Minister George Yeo joined in lambasting the U.S. comment.

"I am quite surprised that the Americans should raise an issue about how we run democratic politics in Singapore when their pork-barrel politics is something of a long tradition," he told state television.
OPPOSITION ALSO CRITICISES PAP CAMPAIGN
The PAP has already won the election, taking 47 of parliament's 83 seats when nominations closed on December 23 because no opposition candidates entered the race for those constituencies.
Voting for the remaining 36 seats takes place on January 2.

The PAP move to link the billion-dollar upgrading programme with electoral choices has been sharply critcised by opposition parties, who say it unfairly excludes opposition-held constituencies from a national programme.

"Voters by and large are not happy with this sort of arm-twisting because they feel the money does not belong to the PAP and even opposition wards do pay taxes," said businessman Chia Shi Teck, who is running as an independent candidate.
Chia said the PAP strategy marked an about-turn from its campaign in the 1991 election when it found its majority reduced to 61 percent -- its lowest ever -- from 62.9 percent in 1988.
"It demonstrated to the ruling party that they'd missed out on the bread and butter issues and there was a lot of anger on local issues not being addressed," he told Reuters.

But while the promise of upgrading might attract the votes of Singaporeans living in older housing estates, Chia said those who had already benefited from the programme would want more and may not remain loyal voters.

"If this election proves anything, it might show us whether local issues really are as important as the PAP hopes they are. Or whether people are going to be angered by this tactic and say, why should we be bullied," said Bruce Gale, an analyst with the Political & Economic Risk Consultancy.
OPPOSITION SEEKS TO FOCUS ON NATIONAL ISSUES
Opposition parties have seized on the issue, saying the election should be conducted on national, not local concerns.
The National Solidarity Party (NSP) said the money already spent on upgrading belonged to the people and the PAP had no right to tie such programmes to election results.

"It would appear that the PAP does not have enough faith in the calibre and credibility of its candidates as it has to resort to unfair tactics to 'win' votes," the National Solidarity Party (NSP) said in a recent statement.

NSP president Tan Chee Kien said the upgrading programme effectively distributed national wealth unevenly by raising the resale value of Housing Board flats, making them increasingly inaccessible to younger Singaporeans.
J.B. Jeyaretnam, leader of the Workers Party (WP), which has fielded 14 candidates in the election, was more blunt.
"This is totally unethical. You use the people's money... It's not government funds, it's not government money. It is vote buying," Jeyaretnam told a news conference.
Government ministers make no apologies for promising better housing, education grants and care for the elderly, saying these will ensure voters make responsible choices.
"We have learned from the results of the last two elections," Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew told reporters after nominations closed.
"We know that if there is no direct stake, everything is the same, then the voter does not take his vote seriously."
